title: Kirby arrangements kept in the players' heads; a possible tribute
summary: After the band broke up, arrangements lived in the musicians' heads; Al Cobb could transcribe them for a repertory project.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I don't know either. I've never heard that one, but I believed that at the time that we recorded -- when we made these albums, Charlie was under contract -- he had a recording contract with Bethlehem Records. And I also think that -- See, Charlie was in his own way, trying to carry on the tradition of the John Kirby sound. Because John Kirby's sound was definitely identified by Charlie's trumpet. And, of course, since Charlie had made most of the arrangements, it is likely that this was basically between Leonard Feather -- it was basically Charlie's idea. Now, whether Charlie ever got a group together to carry on this particular tradition, I don't know. Because Charlie was quite an individual, and he was busy constantly as an individual.

In fact, after the band broke up, you know that Charlie went with Tommy Dorsey.
Offhand, I just don't remember.
Yes. The band broke up and Charlie went with Tommy Dorsey and Procof went with Duke Ellington. Billy was in service. You see, this is what broke the band up.
Yeah.

And, of course, then there was just Kirby and Buster, to try to carry on the band. And it was practically impossible because most of the musicians at that time were not disciplined to play those arrangements. It wound up to be just another little jazz combo. And then, too, I think that those arrangements of Kirby's were never put down on paper in detail. Because of -- especially those jazz classics that they did, Between Loui Singer and Charlie, they would just present a skeletal
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
arrangement, and they worked out the figures as they rehearsed.

So therefore, the arrangements were in the musician's head -- not necessarily on paper. And no one seems to know what happened to those arrangements -- if there ever was such a thing as an arrangement.
But I know that when we were together, and I saw a lot of this stuff that was submitted to the band by Lou, they were pretty skeletal, and they worked the little intricate figures during rehearsal.
And that was to be a very personal thing --
Yes.
(Inaudible)
And it wasn't exactly improvised. I mean, they just weren't thinking. Because they were ensemble, you see. Most of the largest part of the arrangement was the ensemble passages.
And then, too, with that particular
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

instrumentation which was trumpet, alto and clarinet, these were instruments that were all in sort of a high register. And in order to make it sound big, the parts were interchanged there. And the average musician would be thinking horizontally where these guys would have to be thinking obliquely, so to speak.
Yeah.

So therefore, it wasn't a thing that you could just pick up. If somebody could sit down and transcribe these arrangements, which I think somebody is trying to do now -- I don't know whether you're acquainted with Al Cobb.
No, I'm not.

Al Cobb is an arranger, and at one time, he was -- In fact, I did an appearance with him at Carnegie Hall. And he had transcribed the arrangements of 'If I Had A Ribbon Bow' and 'Molly Malone' and a couple of the Kirby things off the
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
record. And if someone would take the time and do that and do Kirby's whole library, they'd have another 'biggest little band in America'.
But there was a lot of discipline involved there. These guys had to be on their toes all the time.
Well that might be a project for one of the jazz repertory companies.

It's a very good-- In fact, there is a certain amount of interest now in that direction. In fact, I got a call from Max Cavelli, who arranges some booking for me at times. And it seems that -- you know, Michael's Pub has a -- When they book a group in now, they usually try to have a theme. They have one composer or whatever.
Tributes to songwriters.
So, I'm sure they want to do a John Kirby thing. And, of course, I put
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Max Cavelli on to Al Cobb in case they're interested. He is the only person that I know at this particular time who's interested enough to putting this stuff on paper, and getting the kind of group together to execute things.

But, it will have to be long-range project, because Al is very busy now arranging for and rehearsing his own large band that will be -- if they haven't already done so -- will be going into the Copa Cabana. And they will be more or less the house band.

But it is a very promising project for anybody who would want to take the time to do it. And, of course, I'm pretty sure that the -- although the arrangements are not available of some of them, I'm sure most of the records are.
Oh yeah.
And they could take the --
Well use the early ones up until about 1942.
Well that's the creme.

That's the best part. Yeah. Because I have, I think, about five albums of John Kirby.
Well that's a pretty good repertoire, you know what I mean?
